page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.1-4 is an entry-tier virtual machine instance configured with 2 vCPUs and 4.0 GB of system memory. Powered by an AMD EPYC 7742 processor running at a base clock speed of 2.25 GHz, the instance allocates 1 physical core across 2 threads using the x86_64 architecture. Memory density is provisioned at 2.0 GB per core, yielding a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. The shape features dedicated CPU core allocation rather than shared or burstable execution threads.

The hardware configuration includes no integrated GPU acceleration and provides no bundled local NVMe or solid-state storage. Persistent storage and data access must be provisioned externally via remote block volumes or network mounts. Network connectivity includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. While no formal benchmark run scores are recorded for this shape configuration, the underlying AMD EPYC Rome processor provides standard multi-threaded throughput typical of enterprise Zen 2 server architectures.

From a cost efficiency perspective, this instance represents a minimal resource footprint tailored for light, consistent compute demands without paying for unneeded memory capacity or expensive local storage tiers. The trade-off lies in the absence of on-box disk arrays and moderate core counts, restricting high-throughput data processing. VM.Standard.E3.Flex.1-4 is appropriate for lightweight web serving, application middleware, API gateways, continuous integration agents, and background job processing.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.1-4 is an entry-tier flexible virtual machine equipped with 2 dedicated x86_64 vCPUs sourced from 1 physical core of an AMD EPYC 7742 processor operating at 2.25 GHz. It includes 4.0 GB of system RAM, yielding a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio. This configuration includes no bundled local disk storage and no GPU accelerators, requiring network-attached block storage for persistence. Network provisioning includes a single complimentary public IPv4 address. With a compact dedicated resource baseline and modest memory overhead, it delivers cost-effective execution for light continuous infrastructure tasks without paying for oversized allocations. It functions efficiently for lightweight web proxies, small microservices, API servers, build runners, and non-memory-intensive worker processes.
